articles.title: Are persuasion researchers working towards dystopia?
articles.authors: Christopher J Carpenter
articles.abstract: A thought experiment is proposed to discuss the difference between theories of persuasion that can be used to persuade anyone of anything vs. theories that can only be used to make the truth more persuasive. This letter argues that much persuasion research aims at developing methods of persuading anyone of anything and questions whether this is a goal that social scientific researchers should want to pursue.

articles.title: Immersive proximity to suffering and crisis: The democratic implications of distressing virtual reality content
articles.authors: Rūta Kazlauskaitė
articles.abstract: Non-fiction VR and 360-degree immersive video are widely used to depict the experiences of victimized, marginalized, and traumatized people, in both historical and contemporary contexts. Immersive VR content frequently engages topics of war and conflict, forced displacement, disability, precarity, incarceration, impact of climate change, and diverse forms of oppression and discrimination. Difficult social topics are introduced experientially, promising the audience an encounter with the lived realities of hardship, suffering, and injustice. The article argues that the democratic stakes of such uses of VR are best understood not by asking whether immersion produces empathy, but by asking what kinds of self–other relations and what kinds of agency are enacted and rehearsed through immersive proximity to suffering and crisis. Drawing on political psychology and indirect-trauma research, I show how immersive proximity to suffering and crisis can shape democratic dispositions via perceived control, threat salience, and victimhood framing. Immersive proximity to suffering and crisis may support solidarity and empathy, but it can also generate personal distress, feelings of helplessness, heightened threat sensitivity, and self-focused victimhood, which may undermine social trust, openness to pluralism, and a sense of civic efficacy. Engagement with distressing content in immersive media should enable reflective processing of difficult experiences, as well as support self–other differentiation, the sense of agency, hope, control, and efficacy, instead of leaving audiences feeling powerless and overwhelmed. The article advances a heuristic for evaluating and designing non-fiction VR depictions of suffering and crisis in ways that support democratic dispositions.

articles.title: Ludo-Iconological Analysis: A new method for reading visual symbolism in games, with a case study on Blasphemous
articles.authors: Baykar Demir
articles.abstract: This article introduces Ludo-Iconological Analysis, a staged interpretive method for examining visual symbolism in digital games through an art historical perspective. Informed by Erwin Panofsky’s iconological framework, the method is adapted to the temporal and participatory conditions of games. While existing scholarship has demonstrated the value of analysing games through artistic sources and visual traditions, the present study develops a more explicitly structured framework for tracing how culturally coded imagery is activated and complicated within an interactive medium. The method is applied to Blasphemous (The Game Kitchen, 2019), a title distinguished by a dense religious visual language rooted in Spanish cultural history. Its symbolic vocabulary draws upon penitential garments, the crown of thorns, public devotional ritual, and historically situated works of sacred art without treating any single visual tradition as the privileged measure of symbolic complexity. This combination makes Blasphemous a particularly productive case for demonstrating Ludo-Iconological Analysis, revealing how historical, theological, and ideological meanings are reconfigured within the visual and interactive structures of the game. By introducing Ludo-Iconological Analysis, this study proposes a focused interpretive framework that integrates established principles of art historical research into the study of digital games. Rather than claiming universal applicability, the article demonstrates how the method can illuminate a game whose visual design is densely structured by historically and culturally coded motifs. The framework is intended as a basis for further comparative application to games in which symbolic imagery is meaningfully connected to narrative progression, player encounter, and interactive context.

articles.title: The challenge of diversity in public service media: A case study of Spanish regional Broadcast Video on Demand portals
articles.authors: Aida Martori Munsant, Tania Fernández-Lombao, Azahara Cañedo
articles.abstract: As European public service media (PSM) corporations adapt to the platformed context, the challenge of preserving diversity, one of their essential elements of public value, has become increasingly complex, especially in the case of regional corporations. In this context, this article focuses on a Spanish case study and examines how the four Spanish regional PSM with Broadcast Video on Demand (BVOD) services – EITB (Basque Country), CCMA (Catalonia), CSAG (Galicia), and RTVA (Andalusia) – integrate diversity in the design and management of these portals (Primeran, 3Cat, AGalega and CanalSur Más). For an empirical and comparative analysis of the strategies, constraints, and tensions that are developing, the study draws on twelve in-depth interviews with the BVOD managers, content directors, and innovation officers of these PSM online services, conducted between 2023 and 2024. The findings show that online portals offer new opportunities to promote diversity as a multidimensional element of public value that goes beyond cultural representation to encompass governance, production, and programming. The study identifies two diversity management strategies – visible and invisible – each reflecting different operational logics that contribute to the renewal of the social contract between PSM and the societies they serve.

articles.title: How platformisation transforms public service media: A new research agenda
articles.authors: Catherine Johnson, Tim Raats, Hanne Bruun, Vilde Schanke Sundet
articles.abstract: The expansion of global digital platforms has significant implications for public service media (PSM), which now operate within a platform ecosystem in which a small number of transnational technology companies increasingly shape the conditions under which media are produced, distributed and consumed. In this introduction to a special issue of Convergence on ‘Comparative Approaches to PSM in the Age of Platforms’ we set out how platformisation fundamentally reshapes the institutional conditions under which PSM operate, challenges the public service remit, reconfigures core values and invites a reconsideration of PSM as a democratic institution. Arguing that this represents a profound transformation, we identify five key dimensions that distinguish platformisation from earlier processes of digitalisation: platforms have created a fundamentally different democratic environment; platforms operate at global scale; platforms create asymmetric dependencies; platforms alter the cultural logics of audiovisual production; platformisation challenges PSM’s normative foundations. Building on the Public Service Media in the Age of Platforms (PSM-AP) project, this introduction argues for the importance of comparative research for understanding this transformation and sets out an agenda for the future of PSM studies based around six core themes: values, ecosystem, audiences, portals, content and role. The introduction argues for the urgency in addressing these themes if we are to understand how PSM—as a systemic intervention designed to drive public and societal value—is to be preserved in the age of platforms.

articles.title: Can’t Name It, Can’t Log Off: Alexithymia and Problematic Internet-Related Behaviors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Fangqing Liu, Xiaoshan Yin
articles.abstract: Alexithymia has been proposed as a ransdiagnostic vulnerability for behavioral addictions, but its role in problematic Internet-related behaviors (PIB) has not been quantified across phenotypes and populations. We conducted a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses. Major databases were searched in October 2025 for studies reporting quantitative associations between alexithymia and PIB (problematic Internet, smartphone, social media, gaming use, or cyberbullying). Risk of bias was appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Random-effects models pooled correlations and standardized regression coefficients; three-level and robust-variance models accounted for multiple effects per study and examined moderators and adjustment for internalizing symptoms. Eighty-three studies met inclusion criteria; 78 independent samples ( N = 42,478; 369 effect sizes total, comprising 302 zero-order correlations and 67 standardized regression coefficients) contributed to the meta-analysis. The pooled correlation between alexithymia and PIB was r = 0.36 (95% confidence interval 0.34–0.38; I 2 = 77.6%). Associations were stronger for addictive-use PIB ( r = 0.37) than for cyberbullying ( r = 0.29), broadly comparable across world regions, and tended to be larger in adults than adolescents. In multivariable models, coefficients attenuated from about β = 0.37 to β = 0.18 after controlling for depression, anxiety, and other internalizing symptoms, but remained statistically significant. Sensitivity and publication-bias analyses indicated that the association was robust. Alexithymia shows a moderate association with PIB across age groups, partly via shared variance with internalizing psychopathology but also through unique pathways. Longitudinal and mechanistic studies should test whether targeting emotional awareness can help prevent or reduce PIB.

articles.title: Victim identity and political consequentiality: Framing migrant and citizen deaths in the Greek press
articles.authors: Nikolaos Lampas, Vasileios Vlaseros
articles.abstract: Why do mass-fatality events with comparable human tolls generate unequal political resonance? This article examines Greek newspaper coverage of two major 2023 tragedies, the Tempi train crash and the Pylos shipwreck, to assess how victim identity shapes evaluative framing, responsibility attribution, and political consequentiality. Drawing on a within-country comparison of three ideologically distinct newspapers, the study analyses how each event was narrated, politicized, and sustained over time. The findings show that, although both tragedies were covered within a broadly negative register, Tempi generated denser evaluative language, more direct attribution of responsibility, and more durable integration into debates over governance and institutional accountability. By contrast, Pylos was more frequently framed through humanitarian, administrative, or border-management narratives and declined more rapidly after the initial news cycle. These differences were patterned rather than categorical and persisted across outlets. The article argues that routine journalistic framing practices help determine not only how tragedy is represented, but whether it becomes politically consequential as a sustained object of public accountability.

articles.title: Centralized hashtags, embedded discourse: Two structural logics of youth climate activism on social media
articles.authors: Yuzhe Zhu, Gustavo Cardoso
articles.abstract: Youth-led climate action increasingly unfolds on digital platforms, where hashtags structurally connect issues, actors, and publics. Using hashtag co-occurrence data (2022–2024) from prominent youth climate activists on X and Portuguese youth climate activists on Instagram, this study applies link community analysis, which captures overlapping multi-membership structures that node-based clustering obscures. Two contrasting structural logics emerge. The international network exhibits a centralized configuration in which core climate hashtags such as #FridaysForFuture and #Peoplenotprofit occupy bridging positions across issue communities, so that visibility and structural centrality closely align. The Portuguese network displays a more horizontal configuration in which climate-related hashtags co-occur with feminism, education, domestic politics, and art-based activism, embedding climate discourse within everyday publics. Digital climate publics take shape as relational structures produced through patterns of hashtag overlap and cross-issue connectivity.

articles.title: Perspective as a Compositional Design Apparatus in Horror Video Games: First- and Third-Person Configurations in Resident Evil Requiem
articles.authors: Ferhat Erdinç Kaygusuz
articles.abstract: For three decades, one question has organised scholarship on perspective in horror games: Which configuration produces stronger horror, first-person or third-person? Comparison across games cannot settle it, because character, space and affordance vary along with the setting. Resident Evil Requiem holds them still: one game, two protagonists, both perspectives and a toggle available throughout . This article reads that design through close playing across four configurations. The perspective never alters what a player-character can do. It alters what the player is permitted to know about the body she is operating: its condition, its capability and its bearing. The same setting carries opposite affective values across the two protagonists, and across Grace herself once she is armed. The reach of the setting narrows as the range of action widens. Perspective is a compositional apparatus, and what it produces is set by the point of action it frames.

articles.title: Toward a Ludology of Fascism
articles.authors: Maxim Tvorun-Dunn
articles.abstract: In a recruitment ad for the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a screenshot from the video game Halo was overlaid with the text “destroy the flood,” presenting an invitation to take part in exterminatory border violence as a form of play. Observing the disquieting glee with which border violence is promoted and conducted in the United States, this paper proposes that fascism should be read as a form of play. This paper looks to games studies as a means to examine how the racialized violence of American policing is given mechanics and procedures that render such violence as pleasurable. Through a case study of the 2023 SWAT-themed video game Ready or Not , this article discusses how thought patterns of fascism are simulated through game mechanics that present fascist praxis as desirable.

articles.title: From Hosting to Authorship: Saudi Press Coverage of the Esports World Cup 2025
articles.authors: Omar Daoudi, Sara Kreishan, Khaled Zamoum, Assel Kamza, Nassir Bouali, Hany Beshr
articles.abstract: Saudi Arabia has made esports a centerpiece of its Vision 2030 transformation. In 2025, it hosted the Esports World Cup, the largest event in the sport's history, in Riyadh. This article asks how the Saudi press constructs the Kingdom through its coverage of that event. Using constructivist grounded theory, we analyzed 57 Arabic-language newspaper articles published during the tournament. We find that the coverage does not simply report the competition. It repositions the Kingdom from the host that receives the world to the author and leader of a global field. A process we call “ hosting as authorship ,” built by magnifying the event, nationalizing it through the leader and the nation, and reframing esports as a field worth leading. The construction is genre-bound and addressed inward, to a domestic public. We relate this inward narration to debates on nation branding, soft power and political legitimacy, showing how esports hosting can be narrated as a source of domestic legitimacy and not only external image-building.

articles.title: Disentangling gender stereotypes and gender inequality in Africa's digital sector
articles.authors: Winfred I. Onyas, Samuel Dawa, George Acheampong
articles.abstract: Purpose This paper investigates how gender stereotypes evolve in Africa's digital space and how digital gender inequality can be collaboratively tackled. Design/methodology/approach A two-phase qualitative study was undertaken, involving consultations with 21 experts and interviews with 30 women in the digital sectors in Uganda and Ghana. Underpinned by technofeminism, actor-network theory (ANT) and social role theories, we examine gender stereotypes as outcomes of dual processes that instigate interconnections among heterogeneous actors in the digital space and accord collective agency to the composite to enact digital gender inequality. Findings The findings reveal that gender stereotypes in the digital sector are tied to gendered narratives and evaluations, which dampen women's aspirations and undermine their confidence. Addressing gender stereotypes and digital gender inequality will require inclusive women-led training approaches as well as heightened visibility of female role models, supported by coordinated efforts anchored in stakeholder collaboration and dialogue. Practical implications The framework we develop is useful in guiding academics, practitioners and policymakers in collaboratively addressing digital gender inequality. Originality/value We make an original attempt to integrate technofeminism and ANT frameworks by employing the concept of agencing to better understand how gender stereotypes are enacted and sustained within an actor-network. Contributing to technofeminist Information Systems research, we reconceptualize socio-technical inequality as dynamic and processual, with gendered power embedded in evolving socio-technical processes, and position technofeminism as a habilitative, interventionist approach that organizes actors to reconfigure digital ecosystems.

articles.title: Blaming the algorithm when losing: how matchmaking algorithm salience affects gameplay enjoyment through internal attribution
articles.authors: Will Zhiyuan Zhang, Ben Marder, Kirsten Cowan
articles.abstract: Purpose This research examines how the salience of matchmaking algorithms (i.e. the extent to which these algorithms are cognitively prominent during gameplay) affects users' experience in online competitive gaming. Design/methodology/approach An exploratory sequential mixed-methods design is employed. In the qualitative phase, semi-structured interviews were conducted to explore how matchmaking algorithm salience shapes players' gameplay experience. From this, a process model emerged and was tested in the quantitative phase using a quasi-field survey with a retrospective recall design. Findings This research shows that the mere salience of the matchmaking algorithm, irrespective of its actual interference, can influence users' gameplay experience. Specifically, when the matchmaking algorithm is more salient, users are more likely to attribute a loss to external factors (i.e. the matchmaking algorithm), which in turn is associated with lower gameplay enjoyment. This effect is pronounced when the game outcome is a loss but not when it is a win. Originality/value This research is the first to examine matchmaking algorithm salience in online gaming. It contributes to human–algorithm interaction research by demonstrating that algorithm salience, an attentional process, conditions how players interpret game outcomes and assign responsibility, revealing a design–experience paradox with broader implications for contexts where algorithmic systems operate in the background.

articles.title: From prompt to profession: how ChatGPT usage relates to students' perceived employability through skill development
articles.authors: Bahar Javadi Khasraghi, Qiuli Su, Hanieh Javadi Khasraghi
articles.abstract: Purpose The proliferation of generative AI tools like ChatGPT is transforming higher education, yet evidence of their impact on students' career readiness remains limited. Existing studies often rely on localized samples and emphasize usage frequency over underlying mechanisms. This study investigates how ChatGPT usage relates to students' perceived employability, focusing on perceived proficiency (e.g. writing, communication) and analytical skills (e.g. critical thinking, problem-solving) as mediators. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Self-Perception Theory and Human Capital Theory, with the Technology Acceptance Model providing a conceptual starting point for understanding technology engagement, we use structural equation modeling (SEM) to analyze survey data from 21,716 students across 100 countries, examining associations among ChatGPT use, perceived proficiency and analytical skill development, and perceived employability, with mediation through the two skills. Findings ChatGPT use is positively associated with both skill domains; however, only perceived proficiency is significantly associated with perceived employability. The indirect effect via proficiency is significant, whereas the indirect effect via analytical skills is not, and the direct path from ChatGPT use to employability is nonsignificant, consistent with a full-mediation model. Multi-group analyses indicate stronger effects for students from low- and lower-middle-income countries and for female students, with no substantive differences by field of study. Originality/value This study provides large-scale, theory-driven evidence linking ChatGPT use to perceived skill development and employability. These findings suggest that structured, critical engagement with AI tools may support skill development without displacing deeper learning. It offers critical insights for higher education policy and pedagogy in the GenAI era.

articles.title: Beyond continuance: how FinTech app experiences shape user well-being
articles.authors: Ali Raza, Shehab Abdulhabib Saeed Alzaeemi, Mousa Albashrawi, Yogesh K. Dwivedi, Inyoung Chae
articles.abstract: Purpose This study examines how users' everyday experiences with digital wallet apps, as a major category of FinTech applications, shape their well-being rather than focusing only on continued use. Using real user reviews from Saudi Arabia, it identifies four key experiential factors: complaint handling effectiveness, perceived system reliability, information ambiguity, and user autonomy. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the study explains how these factors shape user well-being. Design/methodology/approach We applied a sequential mixed-methods design guided by Computational User Feedback Analytics (CUFA) to Arabic and English reviews collected from the Google Play Store and Apple App Store. CUFA integrates hierarchical clustering, Latent Dirichlet Allocation( topic modeling, sentiment analysis, multi-model classification, human validation, and regularized regression. We interpreted the review-derived constructs through SDT and tested them using Ridge and Lasso regression. Findings Our findings indicate that complaint handling effectiveness, perceived system reliability, and user autonomy positively shape user well-being. In contrast, information ambiguity negatively affects user well-being. Originality/value Unlike prior studies that rely predominantly on structured surveys and predefined adoption models, this study applies CUFA to derive, validate, and test theoretically meaningful constructs using large-scale, unsolicited user feedback. It also extends SDT into the fintech context by showing how specific digital wallet experiences support or frustrate users' psychological needs.

articles.title: Toward fairer large language models: a divergence-reflection-convergence framework for mitigating cognitive bias
articles.authors: Wei Liu, Yixin Zhang
articles.abstract: Purpose Cognitive bias in large language models (LLMs) undermines their reliability due to the practical limitations of existing mitigation methods. This study introduces a divergence-reflection-convergence (DRC) framework, which leverages a computationally efficient and inference-time strategy designed to identify and mitigate cognitive biases without costly retraining. Design/methodology/approach This study proposes a novel three-stage DRC framework utilizing a competitive reasoning process where the model first generates divergent viewpoints, subsequently reflects on them to extract a decision rule, and finally converges on a robust output. Furthermore, we validate the DRC framework on five popular LLMs across four common dimensions of cognitive bias, quantifying performance with evaluation metrics including asymmetric kappa (AK) and total variation distance (TVD). Findings The experimental results demonstrate that LLMs refined by the DRC framework provide more consistent and reliable outputs across all scenarios. Notably, this effect is more pronounced for mitigating internal biases than external biases, suggesting the DRC framework is highly effective at correcting LLMs' flawed internal heuristics. In terms of specific evaluation metrics, the DRC framework successfully transforms all negative or near-zero AK scores into positive values and markedly reduces TVD scores, both of which signify a substantial bias reduction. Originality/value This study develops a DRC framework as a novel inference-time mitigation scheme for LLM bias that addresses the practical limitations of retraining-based approaches. Its competitive reasoning process offers a scalable solution for deploying responsible AI. Concurrently, we propose a more nuanced evaluation metric, the AK, tailored for quantifying LLM bias in subjective contexts.

articles.title: Academic freedom: defending a public good
articles.authors: Thomas Hanitzsch
articles.abstract: This essay, an expanded version of a Presidential Address delivered at the 2026 conference of the International Communication Association (ICA), addresses the global erosion of academic freedom and its implications for communication scholarship. Drawing on a survey of 546 ICA members, the article documents substantial restrictions on academic freedom, alongside widespread occupational intimidation. Most survey respondents have personally experienced hostility or intimidation related to their work, most commonly through social media and personal insults. Nearly half of them report altering their academic practice—e.g., by adjusting their teaching content and research topics or speaking out less publicly. While most attacks originate from the public and political actors, the survey shows that a significant amount of intimidation originates from colleagues and other academics. The essay argues that these findings demand a coordinated collective response, including institutional advocacy, solidarity networks, and recognition of academic freedom as an indispensable human right.

articles.title: Associations Between Adult Attachment and Social Anxiety in Romantic Partner Situations: Does Perceived Dyadic Coping Play a Mediational Role?
articles.authors: Kiara Considine, Olivia Beeston, Aidan O’Young, Quincy J. J. Wong
articles.abstract: Adult attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance are associated with negative individual and relational outcomes. However, it is unknown whether these insecure attachment styles are associated with social anxiety in romantic partner situations, and whether dyadic coping may play a mediating role in these associations. The current study tested these possibilities. A community sample of adults who reported being in a romantic relationship ( N = 88) completed measures of adult attachment, dyadic coping style of their partner, and a newly developed measure of social anxiety for romantic partner situations. Attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance were significantly and positively associated with social anxiety in romantic partner situations. Perceived negative dyadic coping partially mediated these associations, whereas perceived supportive dyadic coping did not mediate these associations. These findings suggest that an individual’s insecure attachment style is associated with higher social anxiety levels in relation to their romantic partner, and this association is in part accounted for by the perception of negative dyadic coping of the partner in response to stressors within the relationship. The findings also highlight the importance of relationship-based mediators in explaining links between insecure adult attachment styles and their outcomes.

articles.title: What Makes Child Harm Newsworthy? Event Characteristics, Victim Characteristics, and Media Attention
articles.authors: Nikolay Ternov, Kuralay Mukhambetova, Zeinep Abetova
articles.abstract: Media coverage shapes public understanding of social problems, yet harmful events receive uneven attention even when they involve children. This study examines factors shaping media visibility of child harm in Kazakhstan. Using a corpus of more than 230,000 Telegram news posts (2020–2025), we identify 1,571 incidents involving harm to children and estimate negative binomial regression models to test explanations derived from news values and ideal victim theory. Results show that event characteristics predict media attention more strongly than victim characteristics. Fatal interpersonal violence receives more coverage, while systemic failures receive less. Victim age and gender are not significant predictors.

articles.title: Stories that Make Hawks? Digital News-Based User-Generated Content and Foreign Policy Orientations Among China’s Generation Z
articles.authors: Yang Li, Ying Hooi Khoo, Siti Ezaleila Binti Mustafa
articles.abstract: This study examines the relationships between exposure to news-based user-generated content on Bilibili and Chinese Generation Z’s support for hawkish foreign policies. Guided by the Narrative Policy Framework, a survey ( N = 688) shows that self-reported exposure to villain, hero, and mixed narrative strategies is positively associated with hawkish orientations, both directly and indirectly through national pride and national humiliation. These findings suggest that, within the highly performative and affectively embedded dynamics of social media, nonofficial actors may rely on dramatized storytelling and serve as a nonnegligible component of the broader rise of hawkishness within Chinese youth communities.

articles.title: The False Will Set You Free: How Lower Courts Have Translated the Supreme Court’s Latest Falsity Doctrine into Practice
articles.authors: Robert L. Kerr
articles.abstract: This study provides the first descriptive mapping of the impact of the First Amendment’s rationale for advancing truth-seeking being extended counter-intuitively to provide greater protection for intentional falsehoods. Scholarly concerns over the Supreme Court’s Alvarez ruling focused on potentially creating a doctrinal vacuum of limited guidance. The study found lower courts reflected more clarity of guidance when cases involved the sorts of historically unprotected categories of false expression targeting harm beyond falsity—but considerably less so in other types of cases where it was often “not entirely clear what level of scrutiny is appropriate for laws that criminalize lying.”

articles.title: Do Malaysian Newsrooms Jump on the AI Bandwagon? Empirical Evidence From Journalists’ Perspectives
articles.authors: Jiankun Gong, Yu Zuo, Nur Izzati Aziz, Mumtaz Aini Alivi, Kunjin Luo, Yuqing Lin
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly promoted as a transformative force in journalism, yet most research on newsroom AI adoption remains concentrated in Western and other well-resourced media settings. This study examines how AI is interpreted, organized, and used in Malaysian newsrooms, offering insight from an emerging Southeast Asian media context. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 20 journalists across six Malaysian news organizations, the article investigates how national AI governance signals are translated into newsroom norms, how organizational resources and managerial priorities shape uptake, and how AI is incorporated into everyday reporting, editing, and verification. The analysis shows that AI adoption in Malaysian newsrooms is uneven and selective rather than uniform. First, national AI momentum has not yet produced strong newsroom-level governance; instead, the practice remains shaped by limited written rules, selective disclosure, and strong human accountability. Second, organizational capacity is patchy, with uneven access to tools, training, and infrastructural support across organizations and roles. Third, AI is used mainly in bounded, assistive tasks such as transcription, translation, summarization, and headline generation, while verification labor is redistributed rather than reduced. The findings identify a typology of newsroom responses—cautious minimalists, experimental pragmatists, and human-gated adopters—showing that Malaysian newsrooms are not simply “jumping on the AI bandwagon,” but engaging AI pragmatically under uneven governance and resource conditions.

articles.title: “I’m Here to Work and Not to Call”: Blue-Collar Workers Navigating Interruptions by Mobile Devices
articles.authors: Floor Fiers
articles.abstract: In blue-collar work, such as construction and landscaping, mobile devices allow for communication across dispersed workplaces while posing risks to worker outcomes, including physical safety. When mobile devices interrupt workers, they are tasked with making rapid decisions about how to respond. This study examines how blue-collar workers experience and navigate interruptions by mobile communication technologies. Based on 46 semi-structured interviews nested in a phone survey of employees of a blue-collar company in the Netherlands, results reveal that when interrupted by their mobile devices, workers engage in a complex negotiation process in which they weigh a myriad of contextual factors and consider different response options. Participants describe three general strategies to approach these negotiations: devising rules to guide their choices, taking preventative measures to limit the choices they need to make, and structurally deprioritizing mobile communication altogether. Ultimately, the study highlights that managing interruptions in high-risk environments constitutes a complex skill, one that demands more scholarly and managerial attention.

articles.title: Beyond Seamlessness: Mobile AI and Situated Sense-Making
articles.authors: Thilo von Pape
articles.abstract: This commentary explores what it means for generative artificial intelligence (AI) to become mobile, as interaction shifts from screen-bound querying to AI participation in the flow of everyday situations. Rather than framing this shift in terms of access or use, it approaches mobile AI through situated sense-making, understood here in terms of the constitution of sense through ongoing activities, embodied cues, social coordination, and mobile communication affordances as AI becomes part of the situation. Starting from a café interaction staged in a promotional video for a future AI device, the commentary confronts corporate claims of seamless interaction with theoretical accounts of situated sense-making. Drawing on mobile communication studies and human–machine communication (HMC), it argues that mobile AI requires a specification of sense-making as HMC's central boundary object: not only as mutual interpretation between users and interfaces but also as a process embedded in ongoing activities and interactions. The commentary develops this argument through three interrelated aspects of situated sense-making—coordination, distribution, and stabilization—showing how mobile AI may reshape participation, redistribute epistemic authority, and steer relevance toward either shared problematization or premature closure. It thereby advances an approach to analyzing and designing embodied AI that foregrounds visible coordination, responsive alignment, and stabilization that remains open to collective deliberation.

articles.title: Stress and self-efficacy under artificial intelligence disruption: A mixed-methods study on the usage of artificial intelligence among Finnish workers
articles.authors: Atte Oksanen, Teo Keipi, Moona Heiskari, Iina Savolainen
articles.abstract: Rapid workplace integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping work practices and challenging employees’ self-efficacy and well-being. This mixed-methods study examines these experiences using national survey data ( N = 2109) and qualitative interviews ( N = 54) with Finnish workers. Frequent AI use, AI-induced identity threat, and organizational AI deployment are associated with higher AI strain, whereas AI self-efficacy relates to frequent use, positive AI attitudes, and subjective well-being. Identity threat moderated several of these associations, highlighting the role of professional identity in AI-related experiences. Analysis drawing on Greimas’ semiotic modalities (must, can, know, and want) explains how these patterns are interpreted and negotiated in practice, revealing tensions between perceived self-efficacy and pressures to integrate AI. AI use was often described as voluntary. However, participants anticipated increasing competence demands and responsibility. The findings emphasize the need for organizational strategies that address identity-related challenges and support employee well-being in AI-driven work transformations.

articles.title: Norwegian party leaders’ communication on social media platforms during Covid-19 lockdowns: A longitudinal comparison of Facebook and Instagram content
articles.authors: Roy Aulie Jacobsen
articles.abstract: Social media platforms became key channels for political leaders’ crisis communication during the Covid-19 pandemic. In this article, I examine how Norwegian party leaders used Facebook and Instagram across three national lockdowns in Norway. A dataset of 2,397 posts from national party leaders was coded using a four-part framework for analysing government communication on social media platforms, capturing information provision, input-seeking, politics, and symbolic presentation. Post-level linear probability models estimate how the probability of each communication type varied by platform and lockdown period, controlling for government or opposition status and Covid-19 relatedness. Facebook accounts for a larger share of posts and carries a broader crisis-communication repertoire, particularly for political and input-seeking communication. The use of Instagram for crisis communication became more selective over time, with several communication types declining during the third lockdown. Contrary to participatory expectations, input-seeking decreased as the crisis persisted. Opposition leaders relied more on information provision across platforms, consistent with visibility and accountability work during prolonged crisis governance.

articles.title: Are Chinese scientists willing to engage with the public on genetically modified foods?
articles.authors: Yixuan Guo, Marcia D. de Barcellos, Lawton L. Nalley, Hans De Steur
articles.abstract: Drawing on survey data from 321 Chinese scientists, this study investigates their willingness to engage on a controversial topic, namely, genetically modified foods. Extending the Theory of Planned Behavior with topic-specific beliefs, we analyze how six key factors shape engagement intentions: attitudes toward public engagement, perceived institutional and peer climates, perceived self-efficacy, scientists’ own attitude toward genetically modified foods, and their perception of public attitudes toward genetically modified foods. Results of partial least squares structural equation modeling reveal that attitude toward public engagement and perceived self-efficacy are the strongest predictors, while subjective norms play a limited role. Crucially, scientists’ own favorable attitudes toward genetically modified foods exert an indirect, positive effect on their engagement intentions. We further examine disciplinary differences in public engagement beliefs and find that agricultural and biological scientists hold significantly more positive attitudes toward engaging the public on genetically modified foods than scientists in other disciplines.

articles.title: Shaping science and society through law: Governance logic and public roles in the revised Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Popularization of Science and Technology
articles.authors: Rongrong Ren, Bingyuan Chen, Zhaoyang Sun
articles.abstract: In this article, the 2002 and 2024 revised editions of the Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Popularization of Science and Technology (“the Law”) are examined to explore how the state shapes the science–society relationship. Relevant explanatory reports on the revision of the Law, policies, and central/local materials about the implementation of the first “National Science Popularization Month” are reviewed. Based on four dimensions (political–normative, organizational–responsibility, capacity–instrument, and oversight–accountability), the new Law is proposed to promote science popularization from “an educational and cultural activity to cultivate individual scientific quality” to “a basic governance project that serves a powerful country in science and technology, Chinese-style modernization, and high-level self-reliance in science and technology.” Three cases of popularization efforts, urban, rural and mobile, reveal that the Law increases the visibility and organizational density of science popularization. However, the materials also reveal that public participation is defined mainly as visiting, experiencing, volunteering, and cooperating with governance, rather than issue identification, decision-making, or cogovernance. Therefore, two concepts, “legalized science popularization” and a “state-mobilized literacy model,” are proposed, and it is asserted that instead of going beyond a simple deficit model or becoming a participation model, the Chinese case presents a hybrid form of science popularization characterized by law centering, multiorganizational coordination and state mobilization support.

articles.title: Careful Dis/Connection: Bringing Digital (Inter)Dependent Relations Out From the Shadows of Autonomy
articles.authors: Sara Van Bruyssel
articles.abstract: Although always-on connectivity affords autonomy, it also creates dependencies on digital devices. Digital disconnection has emerged as a countermovement, with people seeking ‘authentic’ offline reconnection under the discourse of (self-)care. Yet, a pertinent question is whether certain care relations are contingent on digital dependencies between people and, despite being perceived as burdensome, should therefore not be broken through disconnection. Drawing on feminist ethics of care, which understands care as all the work that maintains everyday life, this article examines how care and digital dis/connection practices shape each other. Empirically, it draws on ethnographic fieldwork with 20 adults and analyses three vignettes through a relational framework that follows care occurring in, through and away from digital devices. The findings show that digital well-being is shaped less by individual media use than by the care relations that digital technologies sustain. Experiences of digital dis/connection reveal how connectivity is embedded in often invisible responsibilities, dependencies, and forms of care. Rather than locating digital tensions in technologies themselves, the analysis suggests that such tensions expose underlying challenges in how care is organised, valued, and distributed. In response, the article develops the framework of careful dis/connection to evaluate digital practices according to how they sustain, redistribute, and make visible the care on which everyday life depends.

articles.title: Webs of Ainu Mosir: Indigenous Creative Networks on YouTube
articles.authors: Xanat Vargas Meza, Takumi Yokoyama, Chieko Nishimura, Ryohei Nishida, Yoichi Ochiai
articles.abstract: The Ainu are Indigenous people living primarily in Japan. As they have recently adopted social media, and network-based analyses of First Nations cultural manifestations are uncommon, this study drew on Indigenous and social network frameworks to examine creative networks in the virtual Mosir (the world as viewed by the Ainu). Our objective was to clarify the types of collaborators, their cooperation patterns and relationships relevant to producing Ainu-related YouTube videos. Three YouTube lists of 428 videos were utilised in this study. Publicly available data were downloaded using a YouTube Application Programming Interface (API). The videos were watched and classified, including anonymised data on collaborators. The relationships of the collaborators were quantified and mapped, network measurements were calculated and collaborator clusters were examined. The most frequent types of collaborators were individuals and communities. We also observed that individuals moderately affected network clustering ( p = .002). Furthermore, individuals were somewhat correlated with the average number of ties ( p = .004) and the bridging of clusters through betweenness ( p = .006), with Japanese male celebrities and Ainu people, particularly Ainu women, showing high centrality. As Indigenous rights advance internationally, the virtual Mosir shows how crucial it is for First Nations to participate in multimedia production processes, particularly if such productions are available on social media. Indigenous network frameworks were highly compatible with network analysis, allowing for a more comprehensive overview of Indigenous production processes. This can enhance the multiple knowledges of First Nations, while fostering accountability and reciprocity of their allies.

articles.title: Algorithms of Injustice: An Ethnographic Content Analysis of Black Youth’s Experiences with Racial Trauma Online
articles.authors: Amanda M. McLeroy, Tiera Tanksley
articles.abstract: This study explores the pervasive presence of racially traumatic content (RTC) on social media and its profound impact on the mental well-being of Black youth. Utilizing ethnographic content analysis and grounded in critical race technology theory (CRTT), the research identifies key manifestations of RTC, including Black death, digital harassment, deepfakes, and war content. Social media’s algorithmic structures amplify RTC, perpetuating systemic anti-Black racism while exposing Black youth to vicarious trauma, anxiety, and depression. Despite these challenges, social media platforms also provide spaces for activism and community-building. Black youth use these digital arenas to engage in social justice narratives, find solidarity, and develop coping strategies. The findings emphasize the critical roles of educators and counselors in mitigating the adverse effects of RTC by fostering media literacy, digital resilience, and culturally responsive mental health support. This research contributes to evidence-based interventions aimed at empowering Black youth to navigate digital spaces safely, advocate for systemic change, and thrive in an equitable and inclusive online environment.

articles.title: Social Media Platform Repertoires in Everyday Life: Measuring Social Media Use With Passive Metering
articles.authors: Moreno Mancosu, Mario Quaranta, Fabio Torreggiani
articles.abstract: Social media platforms structure the ways in which billions of citizens access information. Nevertheless, to assess social media time use, most research relies on limited data sources, such as self-reported survey measures or behavioral data from single platforms or convenience samples. Using 6 weeks of passive metering of smartphone and computer activity from a quota sample of Italian adults (18–70, n = 1,457), this study provides a behaviorally measured account of platform-specific social media use across the adult population. We quantify time allocation across Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Twitter/X and examine how use varies by sociodemographic factors. Results show that Facebook and YouTube dominate everyday social media time, accounting for nearly three-quarters of consumption, while Instagram attracts comparable average time from a narrower user base, and TikTok shows concentrated usage among younger adopters. Twitter/X occupies a marginal niche. Use is overwhelmingly app-based (>90%), a pattern that browser-based measurement cannot capture. Age is the strongest demographic predictor: Gen Z concentrates attention on Instagram and TikTok, while older cohorts favor Facebook; YouTube shows weak demographic patterning. Gender and education are consistent secondary predictors: women devote more time to Facebook, Instagram, and social media overall, and higher education is associated with lower aggregate use and a smaller share on Facebook and TikTok. Employment and income show null effects. Together, these behavioral, cross-platform figures provide a more accurate basis for weighting platforms by their actual audiences than self-reported or single-platform evidence allows.

articles.title: Automated Influence: How Social Bots Reshape Discursive Opportunities in Online Activism
articles.authors: Linda Li, Helen Margetts
articles.abstract: Social bots are an increasingly prominent presence in online protest discourse. We adapt the discursive opportunity structure (DOS) framework for digital protest, refining its dimensions of visibility, resonance and legitimacy to account for platform-mediated discourse and automated activity. Applying the refined framework through computer-assisted content analysis of bot activity in two major protests – Black Lives Matter (BLM) and Extinction Rebellion (XR) – we move beyond treating bots as a monolithic or uniformly disruptive force, identifying competing pro- and counter-protest strategies distributed differently across the three dimensions. In BLM, pro-protest bot content concentrates on cultural resonance, whereas counter-bot content targets legitimacy; in XR, pro-protest bots are used to build legitimacy and participatory visibility, whereas counter-bots more often work to downplay the movement’s salience. The framework’s granularity discriminates between movement types in ways coarser accounts of ‘political bots’ cannot, showing that understanding contemporary movements requires attending to how automated activity is deployed within their discourse.

articles.title: How Personal Curation Shapes Political Engagement on Social Media? Examining The Politics of Personal Curation Model
articles.authors: Biying Wu-Ouyang
articles.abstract: Although individuals today have a wide range of media choices to engage in politics, recent investigations have revealed that many are increasingly avoiding news and disengaging from politics, especially in social media. From a user-centered perspective, few effective strategies on social media have been systematically examined to enhance political engagement. Established through the curated flows framework, this study proposes the Politics of Personal Curation (PPC) model, which offers a fresh perspective by examining how everyday mundane personal curation in social media (platform expansiveness, content heterogeneity, news attentiveness, and source belongingness curation) have significantly influences on political engagement. A preregistered study from a nationally representative panel in the United States ( N = 1,270) generally indicates that expansiveness, heterogeneity, and news attentiveness curation yield higher political engagement, whereas belongingness curation is linked to lower engagement. This study further supports that these media effects on political engagement are channeled through enhanced cognitive elaboration and moderated by cross-cutting discussion.

articles.title: The semiotics of hope: Visual chronotopes of the community pantry movement
articles.authors: Nelson Mangaldan Buso
articles.abstract: ‘In the current context of global crisis’, Bonnin writes, ‘we have the opportunity to design a research agenda for an uncertain future from a dark present. But there is no reason why that agenda should also be uncertain and dark’. My article takes up this challenge by exploring the visuality of hope. Drawing on the community pantry movement that sprouted across the Philippines during the pandemic, I examine the online representations of these pantries and the ways they mediate and circulate hopeful imaginaries amid the crisis. Using a chronotopic approach, I trace how such visual practices creatively mobilise different spatiotemporalities, thereby suturing the past, present and future, and in effect, registering alternative lifeworlds in the face of systemic collapse. This article contributes to hope studies by rendering visible the visual materiality of hope.
